learning_outcomes: Identify major nutrients in food: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: Chemical components of food needed by our body for growth, maintenance, and energy.
A diet that contains all essential nutrients, roughage, and water in the right proportions for healthy growth.
Diseases that occur due to prolonged lack of one or more nutrients in the diet (e.g., Scurvy, Beriberi, Rickets).

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Principle of Chemical Food Tests
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Specific chemical reagents react with biochemical nutrients to yield characteristic color changes (e.g., Iodine produces blue-black complex with starch, Biuret reagent yields violet complex with peptide bonds in proteins).

key_formulas_and_equations: \text{Energy: } 1\text{ g Fat} \approx 9\text{ kcal} > 1\text{ g Carbohydrate} \approx 4\text{ kcal}

activities.title: Testing for Starch in Food Samples
activities.aim: To test the presence of starch in a given food sample (potato slice / boiled rice).
activities.principle: Amylose in starch reacts with iodine molecules to form a characteristic blue-black starch-iodine inclusion complex.
procedure: Take a small slice of raw potato or mashed boiled rice on a clean watch glass.
Using a dropper, add 2 to 3 drops of dilute iodine solution onto the food sample.
Observe any color transition on the surface of the food sample.
precautions: Use dilute iodine solution; concentrated iodine can stain or mask color change.
Do not taste any chemical reagents in the laboratory.
activities.observations: The surface of the potato slice / rice turns deep blue-black upon contact with iodine.
activities.conclusion: The appearance of blue-black color confirms the presence of starch in the food sample.

activities.title: Testing for Proteins in Food Samples
activities.aim: To test the presence of proteins in egg white / boiled pulse slurry.
apparatus: Egg white or ground gram powder slurry
activities.principle: Proteins react with cupric ions in an alkaline medium to form a violet/purple coordination complex with peptide bonds.
procedure: Take 2 mL of egg white or pulse paste slurry in a clean test tube.
Add 10 drops of water and shake the test tube thoroughly.
Add 2 drops of copper sulfate solution using a dropper.
Add 10 drops of caustic soda (NaOH) solution and shake well.
Allow the test tube to stand for a few minutes and observe the color.
precautions: Handle caustic soda carefully as it is corrosive to skin and clothes.
Add exact drop counts of copper sulfate to prevent blue precipitation.
activities.observations: The solution in the test tube turns distinct violet/purple.
activities.conclusion: The emergence of violet color proves the presence of proteins in the tested food sample.

summary_points: Major nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals.
Carbohydrates and fats provide energy; fats provide more energy per gram than carbohydrates.
Proteins and minerals are essential for body growth, tissue repair, and maintenance.
Vitamins help in protecting our body against diseases; Vitamin C gets destroyed easily by heating.
Lack of Vitamin A causes night blindness; lack of Vitamin C causes scurvy; lack of Vitamin D causes rickets.

learning_outcomes: Classify objects around us on the basis of shape, color, and materials they are made of.
Differentiate materials based on properties: lustre, hardness, solubility, density (float/sink), and transparency.
Understand the difference between transparent, translucent, and opaque materials.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The shiny appearance characteristic of freshly cut or polished metal surfaces.
Substances through which light passes completely and objects can be clearly seen (e.g., clear glass, pure water, air).
Materials through which light passes partially but objects cannot be seen clearly (e.g., butter paper, frosted glass, oiled sheet).
Materials through which light cannot pass and through which objects cannot be seen at all (e.g., wood, cardboard, metals).

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Principle of Flotation and Density
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: An object floats in water if its average density is less than the density of water ($\rho_{\text{object}} < \rho_{\text{water}}$); it sinks if its density is greater than water.

activities.title: Testing Solubility of Solids in Water
activities.title_te: నీటిలో వివిధ ఘన పదార్థాల ద్రావణీయతను పరీక్షించుట
activities.aim: To determine which common solid substances are soluble and which are insoluble in water.
apparatus: Samples: Common salt, Sugar, Chalk powder, Sand, Sawdust
activities.principle: Soluble substances completely dissolve and disperse uniformly among water molecules, forming a clear single-phase solution, whereas insoluble solids settle down or float.
procedure: Fill each beaker half with water.
Add half a teaspoon of salt to beaker 1, sugar to beaker 2, chalk powder to beaker 3, sand to beaker 4, and sawdust to beaker 5.
Stir the contents of each beaker thoroughly with a glass rod.
Wait a few minutes and observe if the substance has disappeared.
precautions: Stir each beaker for equal duration.
Ensure beakers are clean before testing.
activities.observations: Salt and sugar completely dissolve and disappear in water. Chalk powder, sand, and sawdust remain visible; sand settles at the bottom while sawdust floats.
activities.conclusion: Salt and sugar are soluble in water; chalk powder, sand, and sawdust are insoluble in water.

activities.title: Investigating Transparency of Materials
activities.aim: To classify given materials into transparent, translucent, and opaque using a light source.
activities.principle: Transparency depends on the extent of transmission, scattering, and absorption of light rays incident on a material.
procedure: In a dimly lit room, switch on the electric torch.
Place a clear glass sheet in front of the torch lens and look through it at a wall.
Next, replace the glass sheet with an oiled sheet of paper and observe.
Finally, place the thick cardboard piece in front of the torch beam and observe.
precautions: Do not look directly into high-intensity torch beam.
Hold each test material at uniform distance from the torch.
activities.observations: Light passes completely through glass sheet forming a bright spot. Light passes partially through oiled paper forming a dim glow. No light passes through cardboard.
activities.conclusion: Glass sheet is transparent, oiled paper is translucent, and cardboard is opaque.

summary_points: Materials are grouped together on the basis of similarities and differences in their properties.
Grouping materials helps in systematic study and convenient storage.
Materials can be grouped on the basis of appearance, hardness, solubility, flotation, and transparency.

learning_outcomes: Recognize the need for separating different components of a mixture.
Explain methods of separation: handpicking, threshing, winnowing, sieving, sedimentation, decantation, filtration, evaporation, and condensation.
Understand saturated and unsaturated solutions and the effect of temperature on solubility.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The process by which heavier insoluble solid particles in a liquid settle down at the bottom of the container.
The gentle pouring off of the clear supernatant liquid without disturbing the settled sediment.
The process of separating fine insoluble solid particles from a liquid by passing the mixture through a porous filter paper or cloth.
A solution in which no more solute can be dissolved at a given temperature.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Phase Change Principles of Separation
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Evaporation converts liquid into gas upon heating, leaving behind non-volatile dissolved solutes. Condensation cools vapor back into liquid upon heat removal.

key_formulas_and_equations: \text{Solubility } S = \frac{\text{Mass of dissolved solute (g)}}{\text{Mass of solvent (100 g)}} \quad (\text{at temperature } T)
key_diagrams: Filtration setup showing folded filter paper cone in funnel and beaker
Evaporation and condensation of water vapor using kettle and ice plate

activities.title: Separating Salt from Saltwater by Evaporation
activities.title_te: బాష్పీభవనం ద్వారా ఉప్పునీటి నుండి ఉప్పును వేరుచేయుట
activities.aim: To separate dissolved common salt from water using the process of evaporation.
apparatus: Common salt solution (dissolved salt in water)
activities.principle: Water is volatile and boils away as steam at $100^\circ\text{C}$, while sodium chloride is non-volatile and crystallizes as solid residue.
procedure: Pour about 50 mL of salt solution into a clean beaker.
Place the beaker on a tripod stand with wire gauze.
Heat the beaker gently using a burner.
Allow the water to boil until all the water evaporates.
Observe the residue left at the bottom of the beaker.
precautions: Heat gently towards the end of evaporation to prevent splattering of hot salt crystals.
Use wire gauze to ensure uniform heating of the beaker.
activities.observations: Water boils off completely as steam, leaving behind white crystalline solid deposits on the bottom and sides of the beaker.
activities.conclusion: Common salt is successfully separated from water by the process of evaporation.

activities.title: Separation of Insoluble Impurities by Filtration
activities.aim: To obtain clear water from muddy water using filter paper filtration.
activities.principle: The tiny pores in the filter paper allow water molecules to pass through as filtrate while blocking larger suspended mud particles as residue.
procedure: Fold the circular filter paper in half, and then fold it again into a quarter.
Open one fold to form a cone and fit it into the glass funnel, moistening with a few drops of water.
Fix the funnel on the stand and place a clean beaker beneath the stem.
Pour muddy water gently down a glass rod into the filter paper cone.
Observe the liquid collecting in the beaker and the substance left on the filter paper.
precautions: Do not pour liquid above the top rim of the filter paper cone.
Ensure the stem of the funnel touches the inner wall of the collecting beaker.
activities.observations: Clear liquid (filtrate) trickles into the beaker, while mud and sand particles remain behind on the filter paper as residue.
activities.conclusion: Filtration successfully separates insoluble suspended impurities from muddy water.

summary_points: Handpicking, winnowing, sieving, sedimentation, decantation, and filtration are simple separation methods.
Winnowing separates heavier components from lighter components by wind or blowing air.
A mixture of salt and water is separated by evaporation.
More substance can be dissolved in a solution by heating it.

learning_outcomes: Classify plants into herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers, and creepers based on stem height and branching.
Identify parts of a plant and parts of a leaf (petiole, lamina, veins).
Distinguish between reticulate venation and parallel venation.
Demonstrate transpiration in leaves and photosynthesis.
Differentiate taproot and fibrous root systems and link them with leaf venation.
Examine parts of a flower: sepals, petals, stamens, and pistil.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: Herbs have green, tender stems without woody growth; shrubs branch near base with hard stems; trees are tall with thick, hard woody trunks.
The loss of excess water in the form of water vapor from the aerial parts (stomata) of a plant.
The arrangement and pattern of veins and veinlets in the lamina of a leaf (reticulate or parallel).
The innermost, female reproductive part of a flower consisting of stigma, style, and ovary.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Correlation of Venation and Root Type
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Plants having leaves with reticulate venation possess taproots; plants with parallel venation possess fibrous roots.

key_diagrams: Structure of a leaf showing Petiole, Midrib, Lamina, and Veins
Comparison of Taproot with lateral roots and Fibrous root system
Parts of a flower showing Sepals, Petals, Stamen (Anther, Filament), and Pistil (Stigma, Style, Ovary)

activities.title: Demonstration of Transpiration in Plants
activities.aim: To demonstrate that green leaves release water vapor into the air through transpiration.
activities.principle: Plants absorb excess water from the soil through roots, which travels up the stem and is transpired through stomata into the surrounding air as water vapor.
procedure: Take a well-watered, healthy potted plant placed in sunlight.
Enclose a leafy branch of the plant in a transparent polythene bag and tie its mouth tightly around the stem.
Tie the mouth of another empty polythene bag and keep it nearby in the sun as a control.
Leave the setup in bright sunlight for 2 to 3 hours and observe the inner surface of both bags.
precautions: Tie the bag tightly to prevent entry of outside moist air.
Ensure the leaves used are clean and dry before tying the bag.
activities.observations: Tiny water droplets appear condensing on the inside walls of the polythene bag covering the leafy branch, while the control empty bag remains completely dry.
activities.conclusion: Leaves release water vapor through the process of transpiration.

activities.title: Testing for Starch in a Leaf
activities.aim: To prove that green leaves synthesize starch during photosynthesis in the presence of sunlight.
apparatus: Fresh green leaf from a plant kept in sunlight
Test tube containing spirit / ethyl alcohol
Bunsen burner and tripod stand with wire gauze
activities.principle: Chlorophyll pigments mask the color reaction; dissolving chlorophyll in boiling alcohol unmasks the leaf tissue, allowing iodine to react with synthesized starch.
procedure: Pluck a fresh green leaf from a plant that has been in sunlight.
Place the leaf in a test tube and pour enough spirit to completely immerse the leaf.
Place the test tube in a beaker half-filled with water (water bath).
Heat the water bath until all green chlorophyll dissolves into the spirit and the leaf becomes pale/colorless.
Carefully remove the bleached leaf using forceps and wash it in warm water.
Spread the leaf on a petri dish and pour a few drops of dilute iodine solution over it.
precautions: Never heat the test tube containing spirit directly over a flame; always use a water bath, as alcohol is highly flammable.
Wash the leaf gently so it does not tear.
activities.observations: The pale bleached leaf turns blue-black where it was exposed to sunlight upon adding iodine solution.
activities.conclusion: The presence of starch in green leaves confirms that leaves manufacture starch through photosynthesis.

summary_points: Herbs, shrubs, and trees are classifications based on stem nature and height.
Stem conducts water and minerals from roots to leaves and food from leaves to other plant parts.
Leaf venation is either reticulate or parallel.
Roots absorb water and minerals from soil and anchor the plant.
Flower parts are sepals, petals, stamens (male), and pistil (female).

learning_outcomes: Identify key bones and joints of the human skeletal system.
Distinguish types of movable joints: ball and socket, pivotal, hinge, and fixed joints.
Explain the role of bones, muscles, and cartilage in locomotion.
Analyze unique locomotive mechanisms in animals: earthworm, snail, cockroach, bird, fish, and snake.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The framework of bones and cartilages that gives shape, support, protection to internal organs, and facilitates movement.
A joint where the rounded end of one bone fits into the cavity of another, allowing movement in all directions (e.g., shoulder, hip).
A joint that allows back-and-forth movement like the hinge of a door (e.g., elbow, knee).
A body shape tapering at both ends that reduces resistance while moving through water or air (observed in fish and birds).

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Principle of Antagonistic Muscle Action
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Muscles work in pairs; when one muscle contracts, the bone is pulled in that direction while the partner muscle relaxes. A muscle can only pull, it cannot push.

key_diagrams: Ball and socket joint showing pelvic bone and femur head
Hinge joint of the elbow
Streamlined body shape of a fish

activities.title: Making a Model of a Ball and Socket Joint
activities.aim: To construct a functional model of a ball and socket joint to understand its omnidirectional movement.
activities.principle: The spherical head of a bone rotating freely inside a hollow cup-shaped cavity allows full circular rotation in three dimensions.
procedure: Make a hole in the rubber ball and push one end of the paper cylinder tightly into it, securing with glue.
Place the ball into the small plastic bowl so that the ball rests in the depression.
Hold the bowl in one hand and rotate the paper cylinder in all directions (clockwise, counterclockwise, forwards, backwards).
precautions: Ensure the bowl is slightly larger than the ball so the ball rotates without friction.
Fix the paper cylinder firmly into the ball.
activities.observations: The ball rotates smoothly in the bowl in all directions, rotating the attached paper cylinder freely.
activities.conclusion: The model demonstrates that a ball and socket joint permits free movement in all directions, exactly as in the human shoulder and hip.

activities.title: Observing Movement in an Earthworm
activities.aim: To observe how an earthworm moves using muscle contraction and tiny bristles.
apparatus: Live earthworm from moist garden soil
activities.principle: Earthworms lack bones; their segmented body moves by alternating contractions of circular and longitudinal muscles assisted by tiny hair-like bristles (setae) gripping the ground.
procedure: Place a live earthworm on a sheet of moist blotting paper and observe its movement.
Observe the repeated extension and shortening of the body segments.
Carefully move the earthworm onto a smooth, clean glass plate and observe its locomotion.
Using a magnifying glass, examine the underside of the earthworm's body for bristles.
precautions: Handle the earthworm gently without causing injury.
Keep the earthworm moist; return it to the garden soil after the activity.
activities.observations: On blotting paper, the earthworm moves swiftly by anchoring its rear and extending the front. On the smooth glass plate, it slips and struggles to move forward due to lack of grip for bristles.
activities.conclusion: Earthworms require ground friction and bristles for effective peristaltic movement.

summary_points: Bones and cartilage form the human skeleton.
Movable joints include ball and socket, pivotal, hinge, and gliding joints.
Muscles move bones by contraction in antagonistic pairs.
Fish swim using alternating body curves and fins; birds fly with pneumatic bones and modified forelimbs.
Snakes slither in serpentine loops, pushing against the ground.

chapters.title_en: The Living Organisms — Characteristics and Habitats
learning_outcomes: Classify surroundings into biotic and abiotic components.
Distinguish diverse terrestrial habitats (deserts, mountains, grasslands) and aquatic habitats (ponds, lakes, oceans).
Explain specific structural adaptations of camel, fish, cactus, and mountain animals.
Identify common characteristics of living things: respiration, response to stimuli, excretion, reproduction, and growth.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The natural dwelling place where an organism lives and obtains food, water, air, shelter, and suitable breeding conditions.
The presence of specific features or certain habits which enable a plant or animal to live in its surroundings over generations.
Changes in our surroundings that make us respond to them (e.g., bright light, touch, temperature).

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Principle of Biological Adaptation
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Organisms adapt to abiotic factors over thousands of years through morphological, physiological, and behavioral modifications; those unable to adapt perish.

key_formulas_and_equations: \text{Living System: } \text{Biotic Components (Plants, Animals, Microbes)} + \text{Abiotic Components (Air, Water, Soil, Sunlight)}
key_diagrams: Morphological adaptations in desert camel and cactus
Streamlined shape and fins of fish in aquatic habitat

activities.title: Investigating Effect of Abiotic Factors on Seed Germination
activities.title_te: విత్తన మొలకెత్తుటపై నిర్జీవ కారకాల ప్రభావాన్ని పరిశీలించుట
activities.aim: To investigate the effect of water, air, and sunlight on the germination of moong seeds.
activities.principle: Seed germination requires specific abiotic conditions: moisture, adequate oxygen, and optimal temperature to activate metabolic enzymes.
procedure: Take dry moong seeds and soak a portion in water for 24 hours.

Divide soaked seeds into four groups: (A) kept on moist cotton in a warm sunny room, (B) completely submerged under water in a beaker, (C) kept on moist cotton inside a dark cupboard, (D) kept on moist cotton in a cold refrigerator.
Keep group E as dry seeds without water.
Observe all groups daily for 3 to 4 days for radical/shoot emergence.
precautions: Keep cotton moist by sprinkling water daily; do not let it dry out.
Ensure seeds in group B are fully submerged.
activities.observations: Seeds in group A (warmth, light, moist air) germinate vigorously with healthy shoots. Submerged seeds (B) and cold seeds (D) show very poor or no germination. Dry seeds (E) do not germinate at all.
activities.conclusion: Moisture, air, and moderate temperature are essential abiotic factors for seed germination.

activities.title: Observing Transpiration Rate: Cactus vs Leafy Plant
activities.title_te: కాక్టస్ మరియు సాధారణ మొక్కల బాష్పోత్సేక రేటును పోల్చుట
activities.aim: To compare the rate of water loss through transpiration in a desert cactus and a normal leafy potted plant.
activities.principle: Desert plants adapt to arid climates by reducing leaves to spines, drastically minimizing transpiration surface area.
procedure: Tie a transparent polythene bag around the fleshy green stem of the potted cactus.
Tie an identical polythene bag around a leafy branch of the Hibiscus plant.
Place both potted plants side by side in bright sunlight for 2 hours.
Observe the inner surface of both polythene bags for water droplets.
precautions: Use pots of similar size with moist soil covered by polythene to prevent soil evaporation.
Ensure airtight tying of bags around stems.
activities.observations: The bag enclosing the leafy Hibiscus branch collects numerous clear water droplets, while the bag enclosing the cactus stem shows almost no water droplets.
activities.conclusion: Cactus transpires drastically less water than a normal leafy plant due to leaf reduction into spines and thick waxy cuticle.

summary_points: Living organisms show common characteristics: nutrition, respiration, growth, response to stimuli, excretion, reproduction, and lifespan.
Habitats are broadly terrestrial (desert, forest, grassland) and aquatic (marine, freshwater).
Camels have long legs to stay away from hot sand, store fat in humps, and pass minimal dry dung.
Fish have streamlined bodies, slippery scales, fins, and gills to utilize dissolved oxygen.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The comparison of an unknown quantity with some known fixed quantity of the same kind, called a unit.
Motion in which an object moves along a straight line path (e.g., march past of soldiers, falling stone).
Motion that repeats itself after regular, equal intervals of time (e.g., pendulum swing, revolution of Earth around Sun).

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Standard International (SI) Metric System
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: The International System of Units (SI) standardizes units globally; the SI base unit of length is the metre (m).

key_formulas_and_equations: \text{Average Speed } v = \frac{\text{Total Distance } s}{\text{Total Time } t}

activities.title: Measuring Length of a Curved Line using Thread
activities.title_te: దారమును ఉపయోగించి వంకరగా ఉన్న గీత పొడవును కొలుచుట
activities.aim: To measure the exact length of a curved line drawn on paper using a piece of thread and a meter scale.
apparatus: White drawing sheet with curved line AB
activities.principle: A flexible thread conforms to irregular curved contours; straightening the thread against a standard ruler converts curved path to linear measurement.
procedure: Tie a knot near one end of the thread and place it at the starting point A of the curved line.
Using thumb and forefinger, place a small portion of the thread strictly along the curve.
Step-by-step, trace the entire curved line with the thread until you reach point B.
Put a distinct ink mark on the thread where it touches point B.
Now stretch the thread straight along a standard meter ruler, measuring from the knot to the ink mark.
precautions: Use non-elastic thread; do not stretch the thread while measuring.
Align the thread closely along the curve in small segments.
activities.observations: The measured length between the knot and ink mark on the ruler gives the exact contour length of curve AB (e.g., 23.4 cm).
activities.conclusion: Curved lines can be accurately measured using flexible thread and a standard scale.

activities.title: Investigating Different Types of Motion
activities.title_te: వివిధ రకాల చలనాలను పరిశీలించుట మరియు వర్గీకరించుట
activities.aim: To observe and classify different objects exhibiting rectilinear, circular, and periodic motion.
activities.principle: An object can exhibit multiple types of motion simultaneously depending on the trajectory of its points and time symmetry.
procedure: Release the toy car down a straight ramp and observe its path.
Spin the bicycle wheel on its fixed axle and observe a mark made on its rim.
Displace the pendulum bob slightly to one side and release it, observing its repetitive swings.
Record the type of motion observed for each object in a table.
precautions: Release the pendulum bob without pushing to ensure true periodic motion.
Ensure the ramp is completely straight for rectilinear motion.
activities.observations: The toy car moves along a straight line (rectilinear motion). The mark on the bicycle rim follows a circle around the axle (circular/rotational motion). The pendulum repeats its swing at fixed intervals (periodic motion).
activities.conclusion: Motion can be classified into rectilinear, circular, and periodic motions based on trajectory and timing.

summary_points: SI unit of length is metre (m).
Rectilinear motion is motion along a straight line.
Circular motion is motion where distance from a fixed center remains constant.
Periodic motion repeats itself after regular intervals.
A rolling ball exhibits both rotational motion and rectilinear motion simultaneously.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: Objects that emit light of their own (e.g., Sun, stars, burning candle, glowing electric bulb).

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Rectilinear Propagation of Light
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Light travels in straight lines in a homogeneous transparent medium and does not bend around sharp edges easily.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Law of Reflection
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection ($\angle i = \angle r$).

activities.title: Demonstrating Rectilinear Propagation of Light
activities.aim: To demonstrate that light travels along straight lines using a rubber tube and candle.
apparatus: Straight flexible rubber/plastic tube (about 30 cm long)
activities.principle: Light rays travel in straight paths; if the straight path is physically obstructed or curved, light cannot reach the observer's eye.
procedure: Fix a lighted candle firmly on a table in a dark room.
Hold the rubber tube straight and look through it at the candle flame with one eye.
Now bend the rubber tube slightly in the middle and attempt to look at the candle flame again.
precautions: Keep candle away from flammable materials.
Do not touch hot candle wax or flame.
activities.observations: The candle flame is clearly visible through the straight tube. When the tube is bent, the flame is completely invisible.
activities.conclusion: Light travels only along straight lines (rectilinear propagation) and cannot bend through a curved tube.

activities.title: Construction and Working of a Pinhole Camera
activities.title_te: సూదిబెజ్జం కెమెరా (పిన్ హోల్ కెమెరా) తయారీ మరియు పరిశీలన
activities.aim: To construct a pinhole camera and observe the inverted images of bright objects.
apparatus: Two cardboard boxes (one slightly smaller sliding inside the other)
activities.principle: Light rays from each point of a brightly lit object pass through the tiny pinhole in straight lines, intersecting and forming an inverted image on the translucent screen.
procedure: Cut open one opposite side of both boxes.
On the outer larger box, make a small pinhole in the middle of the closed face.
On the inner smaller box, cut out a square from the closed face and paste butter paper over it as a screen.
Slide the smaller box inside the larger box with the butter paper screen facing inwards.
Point the pinhole at a brightly lit distant tree or building in sunlight and adjust the sliding box until a sharp image appears on the butter paper screen.
precautions: Make the pinhole clean, circular, and very small.
Cover the user's head with dark cloth if surrounding light interferes with observation.
activities.observations: An upside-down (inverted), colored image of the distant tree appears on the translucent screen.
activities.conclusion: A pinhole camera forms real, inverted images because light travels strictly in straight lines.

summary_points: Opaque objects block light and form shadows.
A shadow requires a source of light, an opaque object, and a screen.
A shadow only shows the silhouette/outline of an object, not its color or internal details.
Pinhole cameras form inverted images.
Mirrors reflect light, producing clear upright images with lateral inversion.

learning_outcomes: Identify the parts and terminals of an electric cell (metal cap positive, metal disc negative).
Describe the construction of an incandescent bulb (filament, terminals).
Build an electric circuit and distinguish between closed (complete) and open circuits.
Design and construct an electric switch using simple materials.
Classify materials as electrical conductors and insulators.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: A device that produces electric current from chemical substances stored inside it.
A complete closed continuous path through which electric current flows from the positive to the negative terminal of an electric source.
A simple device that either breaks the electric circuit (open) or completes it (closed).
Conductors allow electric current to pass through them easily (metals, graphite); insulators do not allow electric current to pass (rubber, plastic, dry wood).

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Principle of Electric Current Continuity
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Electric current flows only when there is an unbroken, continuous closed loop path between the source terminals; if the filament is broken (fused), the circuit is incomplete and current ceases.

key_formulas_and_equations: \text{Conventional Current Flow: } +\text{ve Terminal (Metal Cap)} \rightarrow -\text{ve Terminal (Metal Disc)}
key_diagrams: Electric cell showing positive metal cap and negative metal disc terminals
Electric bulb showing coiled tungsten filament and lead wires
Complete closed circuit vs open circuit with switch

activities.title: Making an Electric Bulb Glow in a Simple Circuit
activities.title_te: సరళ విద్యుత్ వలయం ద్వారా బల్బును వెలిగించుట
activities.aim: To construct a simple electric circuit using a cell, connecting wires, and a small torch bulb.
activities.principle: An electric bulb glows when electrical energy transforms into heat and light energy as current flows through its resistive filament in a closed circuit.
procedure: Take two lengths of insulated copper wire and remove about 1 cm of plastic insulation from each end.
Fix one stripped end of wire 1 to the positive metal cap of the cell using insulating tape.
Fix one stripped end of wire 2 to the negative metal disc of the cell.
Connect the other two free stripped ends of the wires to the two terminals of the bulb holder.
Observe whether the bulb glows.
precautions: Never connect the two terminals of the electric cell directly to each other without a bulb, as the cell will discharge rapidly.
Ensure wire ends are cleanly stripped of enamel or plastic insulation.
activities.observations: When both wires make firm contact with the cell terminals and bulb terminals, the filament glows brightly. If either wire is detached, the bulb immediately goes off.
activities.conclusion: Electric current requires a complete, continuous closed circuit to flow and illuminate the bulb.

activities.title: Testing Conductors and Insulators
activities.aim: To identify which materials are electrical conductors and which are insulators using a conduction tester circuit.
apparatus: Connecting wires with alligator clips / free ends A and B
Test samples: Iron nail, Eraser, Plastic ruler, Copper coin, Glass bangle, Wooden pencil lead (graphite), Paper clip
activities.principle: Conductors possess free mobile electrons that allow current flow, completing the tester circuit; insulators lack mobile charge carriers.
procedure: Set up a conduction tester circuit leaving two free wire ends A and B with an open gap.
Touch ends A and B together briefly to verify the bulb glows (tester check).
Insert the iron nail between ends A and B so both ends contact the metal.
Observe if the bulb glows.
Repeat the test systematically with eraser, plastic ruler, copper coin, glass bangle, and pencil graphite.
precautions: Do not leave test objects connected for too long to conserve battery life.
Clean sample surfaces of rust or grease before testing.
activities.observations: The bulb glows when ends A and B contact iron nail, copper coin, paper clip, and graphite. The bulb does not glow with eraser, plastic ruler, and glass bangle.
activities.conclusion: Iron, copper, steel, and graphite are electrical conductors. Rubber, plastic, and glass are electrical insulators.

summary_points: An electric cell has two terminals: positive (cap) and negative (disc).
A bulb has a thin wire called filament that glows when current flows.
Current direction in a circuit is from positive to negative terminal.
A switch is a simple break/make device.
Conductors conduct electricity; insulators protect us from electric shocks.

learning_outcomes: Trace the history of natural magnets (discovery by Magnes the shepherd, magnetite/lodestone).
Classify materials into magnetic and non-magnetic substances.
Identify magnetic poles (North pole and South pole) of a magnet.
Understand directive property of a freely suspended magnet and construction of a magnetic compass.
Formulate laws of magnetic attraction and repulsion and learn how to care for magnets.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: A substance that has the property of attracting iron, cobalt, and nickel objects.
The regions near the two ends of a magnet where the magnetic attractive force is maximum (North Pole and South Pole).
A navigational device containing a magnetized needle pivoted at its center so it can rotate freely in a horizontal plane to indicate North-South direction.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Law of Magnetic Poles
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Like magnetic poles repel each other ($N \leftrightarrow N$, $S \leftrightarrow S$); unlike magnetic poles attract each other ($N \leftrightarrow S$).

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Directive Property of Suspended Magnets
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: A freely suspended bar magnet always aligns itself along the geographic North-South direction due to Earth's geomagnetic field.

key_formulas_and_equations: \text{Poles Interaction: } N \leftrightarrow N \text{ (Repulsion)}, \quad S \leftrightarrow S \text{ (Repulsion)}, \quad N \leftrightarrow S \text{ (Attraction)}
key_diagrams: Iron filings pattern clustered densely at the poles of a bar magnet
Freely suspended bar magnet coming to rest in North-South direction
Magnetic compass with directional markings (N, S, E, W)

activities.title: Finding the Poles of a Magnet with Iron Filings
activities.title_te: ఇనుప రజను సహాయంతో అయస్కాంత ధ్రువాలను గుర్తించుట
activities.aim: To observe that magnetic attractive force is concentrated predominantly at the two ends (poles) of a magnet.
activities.principle: Magnetic field strength is strongest at the magnetic poles, causing maximum accumulation of ferromagnetic particles near the ends.
procedure: Spread a small amount of fine iron filings uniformly on a white paper sheet.
Place a bar magnet on the sheet and roll it gently over the iron filings.
Lift the bar magnet carefully and observe how the iron filings stick to different parts of the magnet.
Gently shake off the filings and repeat to verify the pattern.
precautions: Do not inhale or touch eyes after handling iron filings.
Keep magnets away from watches and electronic devices.
activities.observations: Almost all iron filings crowd densely at the two extreme ends of the bar magnet; very few or almost no filings stick to the middle portion.
activities.conclusion: The magnetic attractive force is concentrated at the two ends of the magnet, called magnetic poles.

activities.title: Making Your Own Magnet (Single Touch Method)
activities.aim: To magnetize a plain iron needle or nail using a permanent bar magnet by the single-touch method.
apparatus: Plain sewing iron needle / iron nail (about 5 cm long)
activities.principle: Unidirectional stroking with a magnetic pole aligns microscopic magnetic domains inside the iron piece in a unified direction, turning it into a temporary magnet.
procedure: Place the iron needle on a wooden table.
Take one pole of the bar magnet (say North pole) and place it on one end of the needle.
Without lifting the magnet, stroke it along the length of the needle to the other end.
Lift the magnet, bring the same pole back to the starting point, and stroke again in the same direction.
Repeat this stroking process 30 to 40 times in the same direction.
Bring small iron pins near the needle to test if it has acquired magnetism.
precautions: Always stroke in the same direction; never rub back and forth.
Use the same pole of the magnet throughout the stroking.
activities.observations: The iron needle attracts the small iron pins, holding them against gravity.
activities.conclusion: The iron needle has been successfully converted into a magnet using the single-touch stroking method.

summary_points: Magnetite is a natural magnet.
A magnet attracts materials like iron, nickel, and cobalt (magnetic materials).
Each magnet has two poles: North and South.
A freely suspended magnet always comes to rest in the North-South direction.
Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
Magnets lose their properties if heated, hammered, or dropped from heights.

learning_outcomes: Recognize that air is present everywhere around us and occupies space.
Identify the components of air: nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, water vapor, and dust.
Demonstrate that air supports burning (combustion) through experimental verification.
Explain how animals and plants living in soil and water breathe oxygen.
Understand how oxygen is continually replenished in the atmosphere through plant photosynthesis.

core_concepts_and_definitions.definition: The thick blanket of air that surrounds the Earth up to hundreds of kilometers above sea level.
Air is a mixture comprising roughly 78% Nitrogen, 21% Oxygen, and 1% Carbon dioxide, noble gases, water vapor, and dust particles.
A chemical reaction in which a substance burns in oxygen, releasing heat, light, carbon dioxide, and water vapor.

scientific_laws_and_principles.name: Principle of Atmospheric Oxygen-Carbon Dioxide Balance
scientific_laws_and_principles.statement: Respiration by all living organisms consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide; green plants restore oxygen through photosynthesis, maintaining atmospheric gas equilibrium.

key_diagrams: Pie chart showing proportional composition of air (Nitrogen, Oxygen, Other gases)
Experiment proving oxygen is required for burning using inverted glass jar over burning candle

activities.title: Proving that Air Occupies Space
activities.aim: To prove that an empty glass bottle is actually filled with air which occupies space.
apparatus: Wide glass trough / bucket of water
activities.principle: Matter occupies space; an apparently empty vessel contains air, which resists the entry of liquid until allowed to escape.
procedure: Take an empty, open glass bottle and hold it upside down with its mouth pointing into the trough of water.
Push the bottle vertically downwards into the water without tilting it.
Observe whether water enters the bottle.
Now tilt the bottle slightly under water and observe what happens.
precautions: Push straight down first without any tilt.
Tilt slowly so bubble formation is observed clearly.
activities.observations: When pushed vertically, water does not enter the bottle. When tilted, large bubbles of air rush out with a gurgling sound, and water enters to take the place of escaped air.
activities.conclusion: The bottle was filled with air; air occupies space and must escape before water can enter.

activities.title: Demonstrating Oxygen is Essential for Burning
activities.title_te: దహన క్రియకు (వస్తువులు మండటానికి) ఆక్సిజన్ అవసరమని నిరూపించుట
activities.aim: To demonstrate that the oxygen component of air is consumed during combustion and is essential for burning.
apparatus: Trough / flat tray with shallow colored water
activities.principle: Combustion is the oxidation of fuel; when enclosed in a limited volume of air, oxygen is consumed until its concentration falls below the threshold to support combustion.
procedure: Fix two small burning candles of equal height on a flat dish containing shallow water.
Leave candle 1 uncovered in open air.
Invert a glass tumbler over candle 2 so its rim rests submerged in the water.
Observe the flame of both candles and the water level inside the inverted tumbler.
precautions: Fix candles firmly to avoid tipping over.
Ensure the glass rim is submerged to create an airtight seal.
activities.observations: The uncovered candle continues burning brightly. Candle 2 flickers and goes out in a few seconds, and the water level inside the inverted glass rises to occupy about 1/5th (20%) of the tumbler volume.
activities.conclusion: Oxygen (roughly 21% of air) is consumed during burning and is indispensable for combustion.

summary_points: Air is a mixture of gases, dust, and water vapor.
Nitrogen and oxygen together make up 99% of air.
Oxygen is required for respiration and burning.
Aquatic organisms breathe oxygen dissolved in water.
Soil organisms breathe air trapped in pores between soil particles.
Windmills harness the kinetic energy of moving air for grinding grain and generating electricity.
